text.p: The following are the main stories from Friday morning's German newspapers:
FRANKFURTER ALLGEMEINE ZEITUNG

- Horror after the attack on a Frankfurt church, suicide bomber identified, police suspect psychiatric illness, say 49-year-old woman who killed two others and herself in a Christmas Eve church bomb attack had underestimated power of the two hand grenades.
- Several eastern German state premiers call for the "solidiarity tax" to be kept in place for many years.
- Many new laws and regulations await Germans on January 1. New rules for unemployed and health care insurance, wealth tax expires.
- SPD says Finance Minister Theo Waigel has giant budget hole, federal deficit for 1996 was 92 billion marks in November, well above the target of 59.9 billion marks.
HANDELSBLATT

- Optimists see the DAX index reaching 4,000 point level in 1997. Securities analysts at banks mostly cautious after year of superlatives in 1996. Survey of 33 banks by Handelsblatt finds that on average the analysts believe DAX will end 1997 at 3,095 points, an increase of 8.75 percent from start of year.
- Retailers sceptical for 1997. HDE retailers association expects with no real growth for 1997.
- DGB trade union association calls for higher taxes to fight unemployment. DGB deputy chairman Ursula Engelin-Kefer says goal of cutting unemployment in half by year 2000 achieveable.
SUEDDEUTSCHE ZEITUNG
- Horror over bloody deed during Christmas service in Frankfurt.
- DGB wants higher taxes to fight unemployment
- FDP political leader Burkhard Hirsch says attacks against Rita Suessmuth dishonourable

- German car association (VDA) president Erika Emmerich says "Our car industry is fighting for Germany's competitive position." Says car branch in Germany has stabilised employment levels at about 662,000
DIE WELT
- Horror over bloody deed during Christmas service
- Support for Suessmuth increases
- CDU general secretary Peter Hintze sends letter to party leaders urging them to work to fight unemployment and help campaign to drum up support for the euro.
